description_en: The Hāṭsinjā stone pillars, which date back to approx. 13th-16th century, are erected on a platform at a dirt road junction on the south-eastern end of the Hatsinja (Hāṭsinja) village. The pillars are erected on a terraced stone platform. Pillar 003 is laying on the edge of one of the terraces. The carved sides of the pillars face south (001) and east (002). The pillars were most likely moved around a few times due to their location along a frequently used track leading from Hatsinja to Sahubada, and their current orientations and locations should not be considered originals.Pillar 001 has been severely eroded. Remains of its carved decorum show a large circle on top. It most likely had a carved rosette. The edges of the pillar are decorated with a frieze of rounded and elongated shapes. The site's best persevered Pillar is 002. It has an eroded rosette on top and a stylizedstūpabelow it, topped by a triangular shape. Unfortunately, no inscription was found on the Pillar. Pillar 003 is flat on the south edge of the platform. The visible side only has many cupules.From the 13th to the 17th centuries, stone memorial pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin. They were erected to honour war heroes (Andolfatto 2019). Hatsinja's pillars bear no inscription. Their typology suggests that they were erected between the 13th and 16th centuries. Furthermore, the presence of astūpaon the Pillar 002 can be linked to the Khaśa Malla period (12th-14th century) and their direct successors in Jumla, who were Buddhist followers or Dharma protectors.
references: REFERENCES Andolfatto, David C. 2019. Le Pays aux Cent-Vingt-Cinq-Mille Montagnes. Etude Archéologique du Bassin de la Karnali (Népal) entre le XIIe et le XVIe siècle . Paris: Sorbonne Université.
